content:
Union Minister for Road Transport and Highways Shri Nitin Gadkari today addressed the 85th Annual Session of the Indian Roads Congress (IRC) in Hyderabad, Telangana, and called upon engineers, contractors, consultants and policymakers to work collectively towards improving the quality, safety, durability and sustainability of India's road infrastructure.
The event was attended by Telangana Chief Minister Shri A. Revanth Reddy, Minister for Roads and Buildings, Telangana, Shri Komatireddy Venkat Reddy, President IRC Shri L K Padhi, Director General (Road Development) & Special Secretary, Ministry of Road Transport and Highways, Shri Sudip Chaudhary, and Secretary General, Indian Roads Congress, Shri Rahul Gupta, among other dignitaries, senior government officials, engineers and industry representatives.
Congratulating the engineers, contractors and officials for their contribution to the development of the country's National Highway network, Shri Gadkari acknowledged their dedicated efforts and technical expertise. He emphasised that continuous upgradation of knowledge, research, innovation and adoption of global best practices are essential for developing future-ready infrastructure.
Highlighting the role of the Indian Roads Congress in setting technical standards for the road sector, the Minister noted that IRC has developed several technical codes, guidelines, manuals and publications that guide road infrastructure development in the country. He urged the organisation to strengthen international cooperation and facilitate greater exchange of knowledge, technology and successful practices to keep Indian standards aligned with evolving global developments.
Focus on Construction Quality and Road Safety
The Minister stressed that quality, safety and durability must remain the foremost priorities in road construction. He called for greater accountability among contractors, consultants and engineers and stated that any compromise in construction quality must invite appropriate action. He also emphasised transparent, time-bound and result-oriented implementation of highway projects.
Shri Gadkari underlined the need to improve the quality of Detailed Project Reports (DPRs), strengthen technical supervision and ensure effective implementation of road safety audits. He urged engineers to identify and rectify accident-prone locations through proper planning, improved junction design, and provision of flyovers and underpasses wherever required. Emphasising the importance of protecting human lives, he called for a collective commitment towards reducing road accidents and eliminating black spots through better engineering and design.
Innovation and Sustainable Construction Practices
Emphasising the need to reduce construction costs while improving quality, the Minister called for greater use of innovative and alternative construction materials. He highlighted the potential of plastic waste, used tyres, steel slag, municipal solid waste and agricultural residue in road construction, wherever technically suitable.
He also referred to the use of bio-bitumen developed from rice straw and highlighted the potential of research and field applications of alternative materials in promoting sustainable highway construction and reducing dependence on conventional resources.
The Minister encouraged wider adoption of alternative fuels and biofuels in construction equipment, including electric, ethanol, biodiesel, CNG, LNG and hydrogen-based technologies. He highlighted their potential to reduce pollution, lower dependence on imported fossil fuels and create additional opportunities for farmers through the diversification of agricultural produce towards the energy sector.
Shri Gadkari also called for greater use of treated wastewater in construction activities, particularly in view of increasing water stress. He highlighted the importance of recycling municipal waste and reusing available resources in infrastructure development. He further encouraged research into tree transplantation and plantation along highways to strengthen environmental protection.
Road Infrastructure as an Enabler of Economic Growth
The Minister highlighted the role of quality road infrastructure in improving connectivity, reducing travel time and logistics costs, and supporting trade, industry, agriculture and tourism. Referring to the Pradhan Mantri Gram Sadak Yojana, he underlined the importance of connecting rural areas through all-weather road networks to improve access to markets and economic opportunities.
He also stressed the need to explore innovative financing mechanisms, including public-private partnerships and monetisation of existing highway assets, to mobilise resources for infrastructure development.
Shri Gadkari urged the Indian Roads Congress to focus not only on developing technical standards and guidelines but also on their effective implementation across the country. He called for greater collaboration among the Central and State Governments, research institutions, industry stakeholders and engineering professionals to address emerging challenges in the road sector.
The Minister expressed confidence that the deliberations at the 85th Annual Session would contribute to the development of safer, more durable, sustainable and technologically advanced road infrastructure in the country.

title: Himalayan marmot droppings could reveal clues about climate change
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                19 NOV 2026 5:01PM by PIB Delhi
content:
A new study has probed pollen grains, fungal spores and elemental signatures in the faeces of the Himalayan marmot (
Marmota himalayana
) to trace valuable information on the environmental conditions of the higher Himalaya and how climate change has affected them.
The Himalaya is highly sensitive to changes in temperature, precipitation and snow cover, which can have a significant impact on alpine vegetation and wildlife habitats. Most conventional palaeoenvironmental studies are based on lake sediments, peat and soil. Scientists from Birbal Sahni Institute of Palaeosciences (BSIP), an Autonomous institute of the Department of Science and Technology (DST), explored the potential of faeces of Himalayan marmot as an alternative biological archive for environmental changes with climate footprints. This could be especially valuable in remote, arid mountain environments where conventional sedimentary archives are rare.
The Himalayan marmot, a type of herbivorous mammal living at high altitudes in the cold and dry alpine environment of the Himalayan region, relies on local vegetation for food and shelter.
Pollen preserved in the faeces of marmots has left the footprints of the composition of plants consumed by the animal and provides information about the surrounding alpine-steppe vegetation.
The important plant groups in the diet of the marmot were
Artemisia
,
Asteroideae, Caryophyllaceae, Poaceae, Cyperaceae
and
Chenopodiaceae
.
Fig 1. Field photographs-
a and b.  Alpine steppe vegetation at Pensila Pass in the Himalayan marmot habitat area. c. A Himalayan marmot in their natural habitat in Pensila Pass area. d. Alpine steppe vegetation in Rimkhim area. e. A Himalayan marmot in natural habitat in Rimkhim area. f. Midden faeces of
Marmota himalayana
, g. Shape and size of the marmot’s faeces pellet.
Photograph credits by Hukam Singh, Manish Mehta, and Vinit Kumar.
Researchers Sadhan K Basumatary, Hukam Singh, Manish Mehta, Swati Tripathi, Mahesh G. Thakkar, H. Gregory McDonald, Eline N. van Asperen & Vinit Kumar identified pollen grains and fungal spores preserved in faeces through palynological analysis, statistical methods for comparing samples from two Himalayan regions and Field Emission Scanning Electron Microscopy coupled with Energy-Dispersive X-ray Spectroscopy (FESEM–EDS) to identify elemental composition.
They first evaluated ratios of three types of pollens:
Artemisia
/
Chenopodiaceae
,
Artemisia
/
Cyperaceae
and
Artemisia
/
Ephedra
, for vegetation and climate interpretation based on faecal samples of marmots.
The results indicated that the mixed plant-based diet was dominated by groups like
Artemisia
,
Asteroideae, Caryophyllaceae
and
Chenopodiaceae
, pointing toward alpine vegetation and related environmental conditions. Based on the generated data, it was found that the Himalayan marmot could be a strong indicator species for understanding vegetation and climate changes in the higher Himalaya.
Fig 2. Palynomorphs assemblage recovered from the Marmota himalayana faeces samples.
Ephedra, b. Cluster of Poaceae pollen, c. Cyperaceae, d. Cluster of Asteroideae pollen, e. Asteroideae, f. Artemisia, g. Chenopodiaceae, h. Amaranthaceae, i. and j. Convolvulaceae, k. Pinus sp., l. Abies, m. Sporormiella, n. Podospora, o. Cluster of Saccobolus, p. Pleospora, q. Cluster of Thecaphora, r. Meliola, s. Bipolaris, t. Alternaria, u. Arcella, v. Botryococcus.
This study also confirms that changes in the habitat of marmots can indicate shifts in altitude in relation to changing environmental conditions. This combination of pollen, fungal spores and elemental analysis provides a valuable modern reference for future palaeoecological and coprolite studies.
The study published in PLOS ONE would serve as a modern reference for reconstructing past ecological change and assessing potential impacts of climate change. The findings may also help with biodiversity conservation by improving our understanding of marmot habitat requirements, monitoring changes in the ecosystem and informing conservation strategies for associated wildlife, including the snow leopard, for which marmots are an important prey species.
It can contribute to biodiversity conservation, environmental monitoring, climate research and sustainable management of fragile Himalayan ecosystems.

title: CSIR-Traditional Knowledge Digital Library and Indian Knowledge Systems Division, Ministry of Education, Sign MoU to Strengthen Collaboration on Traditional Knowledge and Intellectual Property Rights
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                19 NOV 2026 11:09AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Indian Knowledge Systems (IKS) Division, Ministry of Education, Government of India, and the CSIR–Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (CSIR-TKDL) Unit signed a Memorandum of Understanding (MoU) today to strengthen collaboration in the areas of Traditional Knowledge (TK), Intellectual Property Rights (IPR), people's rights over traditional knowledge, and the Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL).
The MoU was signed by Prof. Ganti S. Murthy, Professor, Indian Institute of Technology Indore, and National Coordinator, IKS Division, Ministry of Education, and Dr Viswajanani J. Sattigeri, Scientist-H and Head, CSIR-TKDL Unit, in the presence of Dr Raghurama Bhatta, Controller of Administration, IKS Division, and senior officials from both organisations.
The agreement builds upon the earlier MoU signed on 29 June 2023 in the presence of Dr Jitendra Singh, Hon'ble Minister of State (Independent Charge) for Science and Technology and Earth Sciences, and Dr N. Kalaiselvi, Director General, CSIR, and Secretary, DSIR.
Under the earlier collaboration, the two organisations jointly conducted 11 workshops on Traditional Knowledge, Intellectual Property Rights and People's Rights, benefiting a diverse range of participants, including students, research scholars, faculty members, scientists, Army personnel, yoga trainers and project associates. These workshops attracted participants from several States and Union Territories, including Tamil Nadu, Karnataka, Maharashtra, Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, Delhi, Punjab, Jammu and Kashmir, Kerala, Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh, Rajasthan, Puducherry and Chhattisgarh.
The collaboration has also encompassed educational and training programmes, seminars, webinars, conferences, exhibitions and joint publications on subjects of mutual interest, with a focus on promoting awareness, understanding and responsible utilisation of India's traditional knowledge.
Speaking on the occasion, Prof. Ganti S. Murthy appreciated the joint efforts of the two organisations and underscored the significance of the collaboration in advancing the objectives of the National Education Policy (NEP) 2020 and the vision of
Atmanirbhar Bharat
, rooted in
Bharatiya Gnana Parampara
.
He emphasised the need to strengthen guidance on intellectual property aspects of Indian Knowledge Systems and traditional knowledge, particularly concerning patents, copyrights and geographical indications. He also highlighted the importance of developing stronger attribution frameworks to safeguard the rights of traditional knowledge holders and exploring appropriate legal instruments for the protection of Indian traditional knowledge.

title: Council of Scientific and Industrial Research Transfers Indigenous Technologies to Industry to Accelerate Commercialisation and Promote Sustainable Development
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                19 NOV 2026 11:08AM by PIB Delhi
content:
The Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) organised a Technology Transfer (ToT) and MoU signing event at CSIR Headquarters, New Delhi, bringing together CSIR laboratories and industry partners to accelerate the commercialisation and deployment of indigenous technologies. The event, organised as part of CSIR's monthly technology transfer initiative, featured technologies developed by CSIR-Structural Engineering Research Centre (CSIR-SERC), Chennai; CSIR-Central Road Research Institute (CSIR-CRRI), New Delhi; CSIR-Advanced Materials and Processes Research Institute (CSIR-AMPRI), Bhopal; and CSIR-Indian Institute of Petroleum (CSIR-IIP), Dehradun.
Dr N. Kalaiselvi, Secretary, Department of Scientific and Industrial Research (DSIR), and Director General, CSIR, chaired the event.
Delivering the welcome address, Dr N. Anandavalli, Director, CSIR-SERC, highlighted the laboratory's longstanding contributions to structural engineering, infrastructure safety and resilience. She emphasised the importance of translating research outcomes into practical solutions through partnerships with industry. Dr Anandavalli also presented an overview of the technologies developed by CSIR-SERC that were being transferred to industry partners.
CSIR-SERC showcased three important technologies addressing critical infrastructure requirements, sustainable construction and the circular economy.
The Emergency Retrieval System (ERS) for Power Lines, developed by CSIR-SERC, is an indigenous, lightweight and modular structural system designed for rapid restoration of electricity transmission lines following failures or disruptions. The technology was transferred to M/s IFAB Global, further expanding its potential for industrial deployment.
CSIR-SERC also transferred its Recycled Aggregate-based Eco-friendly bricks, Hollow Blocks and Paver Blocks
technologies to the National Automotive Test Tracks (NATRAX). These technologies utilise 100% recycled aggregates and industrial waste to manufacture sustainable construction products, reducing dependence on natural aggregates and promoting large-scale utilisation of construction and demolition waste.
Another significant technology transferred to NATRAX for pilot-scale field implementation was Ultra-High-Performance Concrete (UHPC) Pavement Technology. The technology offers high strength, durability, superior resistance to heavy axle loads and reduced maintenance requirements, making it suitable for developing longer-lasting road infrastructure.
Dr Ch. Ravi Sekhar, Director, CSIR-CRRI, presented an overview of the technologies being transferred to industry, highlighting the collaborative research efforts of CSIR-CRRI with CSIR-AMPRI and CSIR-IIP in developing sustainable road construction materials and technologies.
The MicroReAct-RAP™ technology, a sustainable cold micro-surfacing solution incorporating up to 40% reclaimed asphalt pavement (RAP), was transferred to three industry partners: Innovative Roadztech Private Limited, Delhi; AVK BlackGold Infra Private Limited, Surat; and Hindustan Colas Private Limited (HINCOL), Mumbai. The technology reduces the requirement for virgin aggregates and bitumen emulsion while promoting circular utilisation of road construction materials.
Another significant technology transferred was Bio-Bitumen, developed through collaborative research involving CSIR-CRRI and CSIR-IIP. The technology converts agricultural residues, including rice straw (parali), into a biomass-derived material capable of partially replacing conventional petroleum-based bitumen. The Bio-Bitumen technology was transferred to RAACS Solutions Private Limited, Bihar (BioBhoomi), and SAR Parivahan Private Limited, Kolkata.
MoUs to Strengthen Research and Industry Collaboration
CSIR-CRRI also signed two Memoranda of Understanding to strengthen research, technical cooperation and industry engagement.
The first MoU was signed with the Global Automotive Research Centre (GARC), Tamil Nadu, under the National Automotive Board, Ministry of Heavy Industries, for collaboration in joint R&D, shared testing facilities, technical projects, seminars and academic exchanges. Dr A. S. Ramadhas, Director, GARC, signed the MoU on behalf of GARC.
The second MoU was signed with Pārakhi Skill Systems Private Limited, Patna, for collaborative research in driver risk assessment, cognitive and psychomotor evaluation, field trials, research publications and related technology deployment.
Addressing the gathering, Dr N. Kalaiselvi emphasised that it is imperative for CSIR to transfer more and more technologies to industry, ensuring that scientific research undertaken in its laboratories translates into tangible economic, industrial and societal benefits.
She stressed that technology development must be accompanied by effective mechanisms for industrial adoption, commercialisation and scale-up. The monthly technology transfer initiative, she noted, provides an important platform for strengthening the interface between CSIR laboratories and industry and accelerating the journey of innovations from laboratory to market. The DG, CSIR emphasised that the true measure of scientific research lies in its successful translation into products, processes and technologies that benefit industry and society.
The programme concluded with a vote of thanks by Dr Thallada Bhaskar, Director, CSIR-AMPRI, who expressed gratitude to the Director General, CSIR, participating laboratories, industry partners and other stakeholders.

ministry: Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship
date:

                19 NOV 2026 5:34PM by PIB Delhi
content:
In a significant milestone in the implementation of the Pradhan Mantri Skilling and Employability Transformation through Upgraded ITIs (PM-SETU) scheme, Shareholders' Agreements (SHAs) have been signed for four Industrial Training Institute (ITI) clusters in Telangana with Apollo MedSkills Ltd., Neuland Foundation, ZEN Technologies Ltd. and Sri Siddhartha Infratech & Services as Anchor Industry Partners (AIPs). The agreements mark the commencement of the implementation phase of approved Strategic Investment Plans (SIPs) for the Old City, Sangareddy, Medchal and Patancheru clusters, paving the way for industry-led transformation of Government ITIs in the State.
The SHAs have been signed between the Directorate General of Training (DGT), Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship (MSDE), Government of India, Government of Telangana, and the respective industry partners, establishing the institutional framework for implementation of these projects under PM-SETU.
The four clusters represent an approved investment of approximately ₹1,011 crore, including:
Old City Cluster with Apollo MedSkills Ltd. as Anchor Industry Partner in the Healthcare & Life Sciences sector, with an approved investment of ₹241 crore;
Sangareddy Cluster with Neuland Foundation as Anchor Industry Partner in the Pharmaceuticals & Chemicals sector, with an approved investment of ₹241 crore;
Medchal Cluster with ZEN Technologies Ltd. as Anchor Industry Partner in the Defence & Electronics sector, with an approved investment of ₹254 crore; and
Patancheru Cluster with Sri Siddhartha Infratech & Services as Anchor Industry Partner in the Diversified Manufacturing sector, with an approved investment of ₹275 crore.
The signing of the SHAs formalises collaboration among the Government of India, the Government of Telangana and the industry partners for execution of the approved projects. Dedicated Special Purpose Vehicles (SPVs) will now be established for each cluster to oversee implementation and long-term operations. Under the PM-SETU framework, the industry partner will hold a 51 per cent stake in the SPV, while the Government of India and the State Government will each hold 24.5 per cent equity participation.
PM-SETU Moves from Planning to Implementation
With the signing of these agreements, the four Telangana projects move from the planning phase into active implementation. These partnerships are expected to deepen industry participation in vocational education and accelerate the transformation of participating ITIs into modern, future-ready centres of technical excellence. With this milestone, the total number of Shareholders' Agreements signed under PM-SETU has now reached seven, reflecting the growing momentum of industry-led institutional transformation across the country.
The approved investment plans envisage a comprehensive package of interventions, including:
Modernisation of training infrastructure, workshops and laboratories;
Introduction of industry-relevant technologies and equipment;
Alignment of curricula with evolving sectoral requirements;
Capacity building and training of instructors;
Enhanced industry exposure and apprenticeship opportunities; and
Strengthening of placement and employability outcomes for trainees.
By bringing industry expertise directly into the governance and development of ITIs, the initiative aims to create institutions that are responsive to the needs of key sectors of the economy while equipping youth with skills required for emerging job opportunities.
Smt Debashree Mukherjee, Secretary, Ministry of Skill Development and Entrepreneurship, welcomed all industry partners and commended their commitment to transforming ITIs across the country. She noted that PM-SETU is establishing a new paradigm in skill development by placing industry at the heart of institutional transformation.
Representatives from the four industry partners reaffirmed their commitment to supporting the Government's vision of a world-class vocational education ecosystem and contributing sector-specific expertise across healthcare, pharmaceuticals, defence electronics and manufacturing to enhance the quality and relevance of training delivered through the participating ITIs.

title: Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi Chairs Plenary Session of ‘SAMAVESHI NITI SANKALP 2026’
subtitle:
Calls For Whole-Of-Government Approach To Build An Inclusive, Accessible And Drug-Free India

Centre And States Identify Time-Bound Action Points On Drug Demand Reduction, Scholarships, Early Intervention And Accessibility; Summit Reinforces Collective Commitment Towards Viksit Bharat @2047
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:
                19 NOV 2026 10:34PM by PIB Delhi
content:
Hon’ble Prime Minister Shri Narendra Modi today applauded and commended the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment for organizing the Two Day Departmental Summit and facilitating meaningful deliberations. The Prime Minister emphasized the importance of collective action and a ‘Whole of Government’ approach in achieving the objectives of social justice, social empowerment and a Nasha Mukt Bharat.
Addressing the the plenary session of the two-day Departmental Summit titled
‘Samaveshi Niti Sankalp’
, at the Sushma Swaraj Bhawan, in the National Capital here late this evening , Shri Modi highlighted the transformative impact of the Government’s welfare initiatives, he observed that nearly 50 crore people lifted out of poverty have experienced genuine social empowerment.
Calling for the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan to be transformed into a nationwide
Jan Andolan
, the Prime Minister stressed that every citizen, family, educational institution and community must contribute to building a drug-free India. He encouraged schools to organize essay competitions and undertake awareness initiatives, while sensitizing parents to recognize early signs of substance abuse and addiction.
Emphasizing the importance of rehabilitation and social reintegration, Shri Modi observed that the journeys of individuals who have successfully overcome substance dependence carry a powerful message of hope. “These journeys carry the strongest message of hope. They show that recovery is possible and that a life free from drugs is a life of dignity,” he said.
The Prime Minister also urged farmers to shun illicit crop cultivation and called for coordinated efforts involving all Ministries, State Governments, district administrations and spiritual organizations to strengthen the national campaign against drug abuse.
Recognising the influence of spiritual leaders, the Prime Minister said that spiritual gurus and organisations have a vital role to play in the mission. Their guidance, he noted, can inspire millions to choose a life free from drugs.
On the empowerment of persons with disabilities, the Prime Minister highlighted the significance of the term ‘Divyang’, noting its contribution towards enhancing the dignity, respect and self-esteem of persons with disabilities.
Shri Modi encouraged its wider use and popularization to foster a positive outlook towards Divyangjan across society. He also emphasized the need to identify, nurture and recognize their inherent talents and abilities by providing appropriate opportunities and platforms for their participation and contribution.
The Prime Minister’s address reinforced the need for sustained cooperation between the Centre and States, institutional convergence and effective implementation of welfare programmes to ensure that the benefits of development reach every section of society.
The Summit was attended by Union Ministers for Social Justice and Empowerment, Ministers from 27 States and Union Territories, Secretaries of both Departments, Secretaries from 35 States and Union Territories, and senior officers of the Ministry and participating State/UT administrations, to deliberate on key priorities and strengthen collaborative efforts towards inclusive social development and empowerment.
Four thematic priorities deliberated at the Summit
The two-day Departmental Summit commenced on November 18, 2026, with the inaugural session addressed by Union Minister for Social Justice and Empowerment Dr. Virendra Kumar. Context-setting remarks were delivered by the Secretaries of the Department of Social Justice and Empowerment (DoSJE) and the Department of Empowerment of Persons with Disabilities (DEPwD), outlining the policy priorities and implementation challenges relating to drug demand reduction, scholarships, early intervention and accessibility.
The first day on November 18 featured four thematic deliberations focusing on Re-imagining Prevention and Drug Demand Reduction for Nasha Mukt Bharat; Accessible Scholarships, Empowered Students; Early Intervention and Reduction of Disability Burden; and Sugamya Bharat for Viksit Bharat.
Four parallel breakout sessions provided a platform for Ministers and senior officials from States and Union Territories to exchange best practices, discuss implementation challenges and identify actionable measures with clearly defined timelines.
1. Re-imagining Prevention and Drug Demand Reduction for Nasha Mukt Bharat
The session, chaired by Dr. (Col.) Dhani Ram Shandil, Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment, Himachal Pradesh, and co-chaired by Shri Avinash Gehlot, Minister of Social Justice and Empowerment, Rajasthan, focused on transforming drug prevention and awareness efforts into a sustained
Jan Andolan
.
The key action points included observing the 10th of every month as
Nasha Mukti Sankalp Diwas
, beginning December 2026; making drug prevention a standing agenda item in every Gram Sabha and Municipal Ward; and establishing at least one de-addiction centre in every district by March 2029.
States shared several innovative initiatives, including Chandigarh’s VADA Clubs, Punjab’s SOORMA Ambassadors, Meghalaya’s DREAM Solace Home, Jammu and Kashmir’s 100 Days Campaign and Haryana’s STARS Rating for rehabilitation centres.
Dr. Shandil underscored the importance of structured and continuous interventions through families, schools and communities, observing that prevention is both sound public health policy and sound economics.
Shri Gehlot emphasised the need to move beyond government-led programmes towards community-driven participation.
Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri B. L. Verma affirmed that the outcomes of the deliberations would inform the national action plan.
2. Accessible Scholarships, Empowered Students
Chaired by Shri Asim Arun, Minister in the Government of Uttar Pradesh, and co-chaired by Shri Kishan Kumar Bedi, Minister in the Government of Haryana, the session focused on developing an integrated, accessible and student-centric scholarship delivery ecosystem.
The deliberations emphasized simplification of application procedures, secure digital integration between the Centre and States, assisted application facilities, timely disbursement of scholarships and strengthened grievance redressal mechanisms. Suggestions relating to revision of income eligibility criteria and scholarship amounts were also discussed.
States highlighted successful initiatives, including common scholarship platforms in Odisha, Gujarat and Uttar Pradesh; Andhra Pradesh’s One Stop Scholarship Portal; prior scrutiny of applications in Madhya Pradesh; and auto-approval mechanisms adopted by Karnataka and Tamil Nadu.
The discussions underscored the importance of technology-enabled service delivery, intergovernmental coordination and transparent processes to ensure that eligible students receive scholarship assistance in a timely and hassle-free manner.
3. Early Intervention and Reduction of Disability Burden
The session, chaired by Dr. Shweta Gupta, Minister in the Government of Bihar, and co-chaired by Ms. Pi Lalrinpuii, Minister in the Government of Mizoram, focused on strengthening early identification, timely assessment and intervention for children with developmental delays and disabilities.
The key priorities included strengthening convergence among health, nutrition, education and disability-related services; expanding tele-rehabilitation and mobile outreach facilities; developing integrated digital tracking systems; and enhancing the availability of trained human resources.
West Bengal presented its SANSPARSH model, which facilitates community-level screening for Autism Spectrum Disorder (ASD) through a 20-point questionnaire.
Dr. Gupta highlighted that early identification and convergence of existing services are critical to reducing the burden of disability and ensuring that support reaches beneficiaries at the grassroots level.
Ms. Lalrinpuii emphasised the importance of parental awareness, continuous follow-up and shared responsibility among families, institutions and service providers.
4. Sugamya Bharat for Viksit Bharat
The fourth thematic session focused on mainstreaming universal accessibility and inclusive design in public infrastructure, transport systems and digital services from the planning stage itself. The discussions highlighted the need for regular accessibility audits, effective monitoring mechanisms and active participation of persons with disabilities in the design and evaluation of public facilities.
States showcased several good practices, including Kochi Metro and Water Metro in Kerala, with Indian Sign Language-trained staff and accessible amenities; accessibility upgrades at Chennai Egmore and suburban railway stations in Tamil Nadu, including Braille-enabled lifts, tactile pathways and induction loops; accessible tourist spaces in Goa; level-boarding Ahmedabad Janmarg buses in Gujarat; and mandatory barrier-free infrastructure in schools in Assam.
Minister of State for Social Justice and Empowerment Shri B. L. Verma emphasised that accessibility is not an additional facility but the foundation of equal opportunities and a life of dignity, particularly in the context of the national vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.
Goa Minister Shri Subhash Faldessai advocated incorporating accessibility at the design and planning stage rather than relying on retrofitting.
Assam highlighted proposals for a dedicated National Mission, district-level monitoring and appropriate penalties for non-compliance with accessibility requirements.
Knowledge-sharing and exhibition of best practices
During the full-house sessions, experts Dr. Varsha Gathoo (formerly AYJNISHD) and Prof. J. S. Thakur (PGIMER) presented global best practices from the US, Australia, Switzerland, Iceland, Thailand, and the African Union alongside national policies.
An exhibition at Sushma Swaraj Bhawan showcased schemes, initiatives, success stories, digital applications and portals of both Departments, providing participants with an opportunity to understand innovative interventions and effective models of service delivery.
Renewed commitment to inclusive and empowered India
The deliberations culminated in a renewed commitment to strengthen Centre-State cooperation, institutional convergence and time-bound implementation of the agreed action points.
The Summit provided an important platform for translating policy priorities into coordinated action, leveraging successful State-level practices and addressing implementation gaps through collective responsibility.
With a shared focus on drug demand reduction, equitable access to educational opportunities, early intervention for persons with disabilities and universal accessibility, ‘SAMAVESHI NITI SANKALP 2026’ reaffirmed the Government’s commitment to building an inclusive, empowered, accessible and drug-free India in keeping with the vision of Viksit Bharat @2047.

Access to comprehensive de-addiction treatment, counselling and rehabilitation services plays a significant role in promoting individual well-being, strengthening family relationships, economic self-reliance and social reintegration among individuals affected by substance dependence.
Mr. Sudesh Kumar
(name changed),
a 42-year-old resident of Kadapa, Andhra Pradesh, belonging to the Other Backward Classes (OBC) community, has successfully overcome alcohol addiction with rehabilitation support under the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (NAPDDR) Scheme of the Ministry of Social Justice and Empowerment, Government of India.
Having studied up to high school, Rajesh worked as a driver and also undertook daily wage labour to support his wife and two children. However, alcohol addiction gradually affected his personal, professional and financial well-being, resulting in irregular employment, financial instability and strained family relationships.

On February 5, 2026, Sudesh received comprehensive de-addiction treatment and rehabilitation assistance under the NAPDDR Scheme, which included individual counselling, family counselling, group counselling, yoga, meditation, motivational sessions and psychosocial support.
For individuals undergoing recovery from substance dependence, access to structured rehabilitation and sustained counselling is an important enabler of personal and social transformation. These interventions helped Sudesh understand the harmful effects of alcohol addiction, rebuild his self-confidence and develop a positive outlook towards life. Family counselling further strengthened his relationships with family members.
As per the follow-up conducted on April 27, 2026, Sudesh had completely abstained from alcohol consumption and was leading a sober and responsible life. He had also established a small tea shop in Kadapa, enabling him to earn a stable income, support his family and work towards economic self-reliance.

content:
Reaffirming India’s abiding commitment to partnership and shared progress in the field of official statistics, the National Statistical Systems Training Academy (NSSTA)- Ministry of Statistics and Programme Implementation (MoSPI), in collaboration with the National Institute of Labour Economics Research and Development (NILERD), organised an interaction of international participants from twenty-six partner countries of the Indian Technical and Economic Cooperation (ITEC) Programme on 17 November 2026. The engagement offered the visiting delegates a meaningful vantage point on the manner in which India builds, governs and sustains its statistical institutions.
The occasion was graced by the eminent presence of Dr. Dalip Singh, Director General (Central Statistics) and Dr. Purnendu Kishore Banerjee, Director General (Data Governance)-In-Charge, MoSPI, along with senior officers of the Ministry, including Shri R. Rajesh, Additional Director General, Capacity Development Division and Ms. Supriya Roy, Additional Director General, Social Statistics Division. Dr. P. C. Parida, Director, NILERD and faculty of NILERD also participated.
Setting the tone for the day’s deliberations, Shri R. Rajesh, Additional Director General, Capacity Development Division recalled India’s timeless message that the world is one family and that all people are one’s own kin. Anchored in this civilisational outlook, he stressed that the country has consistently striven to extend its support to other nations in improving and strengthening their statistical systems. Ms. Reena Singh, Deputy Director General, NSSTA, while moderating the interaction, emphasized the crucial role of MoSPI in strengthening the country’s official statistical system ensuring the availability of reliable, credible and timely statistical information, and supporting evidence based policymaking across sectors. She also emphasized the pivotal role of NSSTA for strengthening the capacity of the statistical system in India.
The keynote address, delivered by Dr. Dalip Singh, Director General (Central Statistics), furnished the delegates with a comprehensive panorama of the National Statistical System of India. In the course of his address, he elaborated on the institutional framework, the organisational structure and the functioning of the Statistical System, thereby giving an overview of the various statistical products and varied surveys undertaken by MoSPI.
The substantive core of the interaction consisted of two technical sessions. The first session on “Overview of SDG Monitoring in India” was led by Ms. Supriya Roy, Additional Director General, SSD, Ms. Ruchika Gupta, Deputy Director General, SSD, and Shri Indradeep Roy Chaudhary, Director, SSD. The session provided an overview of more than 270 national indicators identified by MoSPI for monitoring SDGs and its continuous process of alignment with the Global Indicator Framework. The session on “Developing and Managing Statistical Database” was presented by Shri Vishnu Mishra, Director, Data Innovation and Information Division (DIID), MoSPI which provided insights into the e-Sankhyiki portal, microdata portal, semantic search, Model Context Protocol (MCP) micro and macro datasets etc.
Bringing the proceedings to a close, Shri P. K. Banerjee, Director General (Data Governance)-In-Charge, engaged with the international participants and shared valuable perspectives on India’s statistical ecosystem in his concluding remarks. He urged the delegates to carry the learnings of the interaction back with them and apply them towards strengthening the statistical systems of their respective countries.
India reaffirms its unwavering commitment to all participating nations through sustained technical cooperation, knowledge-sharing and institutional partnership to translate shared learning  into actionable outcomes.

A high-level meeting to deliberate upon the Comprehensive Development Plan for Bastar Region was held in Raipur today under the chairpersonship of Shri Vikas Sheel, Chief Secretary, Government of Chhattisgarh. The deliberations focused on developing Bastar as a model tribal region through coordinated, locally responsive and outcome-oriented interventions.
The delegation from the Ministry of Tribal Affairs was led by Shri Manish Thakur, Additional Secretary, MoTA along with Ms. Samidha Singh, Director, MoTA, Mr. Akhila Biharia Ota and Ms. Sweta Mishra, Senior Advisors MoTA and Shri Subhash Kumar, DAJGUA Division MoTA.

Rahul Venkat, Commissioner, Tribal and Scheduled Caste Development.
The Development Plan covers the seven districts of Bastar Division—Bastar, Kanker, Kondagaon, Narayanpur, Dantewada, Bijapur and Sukma. Building upon the Ministry’s engagement with the State and district administration, the meeting provided a platform to examine developmental gaps, identify implementation priorities and strengthen convergence among Central schemes, State departments and district-level institutions, including ITDAs/ITDPs.
Key interventions discussed included community-managed crèches in vulnerable tribal areas; a proposed Sickle Cell Disease Centre of Competence at Jagdalpur; targeted malaria and tuberculosis elimination; mother-tongue-based multilingual education; and adult, digital and financial literacy. Livelihood priorities encompassed tamarind and mahua value-addition clusters, agriculture and horticulture, livestock and fisheries, tribal entrepreneurship, traditional craft clusters, the proposed TRIFOOD Park at Jagdalpur and community-led eco-tourism.
The Plan also envisages conservation of sacred groves and indigenous medicinal plants, promotion of tribal music and crafts, strengthening of the BADAL Academy, recognition of Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Group habitat rights and community forest resource management. Proposals for village electrification and other basic amenities were also highlighted. The Ministry’s presentation outlined interventions at different stages of approval, proposal development and implementation.
The meeting underscored the importance of community participation, district-specific planning, time-bound follow-up and effective institutional coordination to translate proposed interventions into measurable improvements in the quality of life and livelihood opportunities of tribal communities across Bastar.

title: ​​​​​​​Beyond the Screen
subtitle: How IFFI Is Shaping the Future of Indian Cinema
content:
The 57th IFFI in Goa
Source: Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
Cinema has a unique way of bringing people together. A story from a remote village can move audiences thousands of miles away. A film in an unfamiliar language can evoke emotions everyone understands. Beyond geographical boundaries and cultural differences, stories find ways to connect people. Film festivals make these connections possible, bringing diverse voices, fresh perspectives and new talent onto one stage.
This spirit of storytelling takes centre stage at the
57th International Film Festival of India (IFFI)
. The festival returns to
Goa
from
20 to 28 November 2026.
Its theme,
Stories Without Borders
, celebrates cinema's power to connect people across cultures and countries. Over nine days, the festival will bring together filmmakers, emerging talent and cinema enthusiasts from around the world.
Yet, IFFI is about more than the films audiences watch. For a young filmmaker, it could mean a first encounter with the global film industry. For a regional storyteller, it could mean reaching audiences beyond familiar linguistic and cultural boundaries. For an independent filmmaker, it could open doors to new collaborations and opportunities. Through its various initiatives, IFFI continues to nurture talent, celebrate India's cinematic diversity and strengthen global connections.
Nurturing the Next Generation of Storytellers
Every filmmaker begins somewhere, often with an idea and the determination to bring it alive. Turning that idea into a film requires more than creativity. It demands technical skills, collaboration, industry exposure and opportunities to demonstrate one's abilities. For aspiring filmmakers, IFFI offers a chance to take these important steps.
At the centre of this effort is
Creative Minds of Tomorrow (CMOT)
, introduced in 2021. Its sixth edition at IFFI 2026 will bring together
100 young talents across 13 filmmaking crafts
. These range from direction, cinematography and scriptwriting to sound recording, costume design and visual effects. The initiative recognises that filmmaking depends on many creative disciplines working together.
Participants will engage in masterclasses, workshops and conversations with established film professionals. A
48-hour filmmaking challenge
will test their ability to turn ideas into completed films. The programme also includes the CMOT Talent Camp where participants will pitch creative concepts and explore opportunities across the media and entertainment industry. Together, these activities provide practical experience and exposure beyond conventional classroom learning.
Source: Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
The initiative has already seen young filmmakers progress to international recognition.
Chidananda S. Naik
, a CMOT participant in 2022, offers a notable example. His short film,
Sunflowers Were the First Ones to Know
, made as a student of the Film and Television Institute of India (FTII), won the
La Cinef Award
at Cannes in 2024. A Kannada-language film inspired by Indian folk stories and traditions, it demonstrated the international appeal of locally inspired storytelling. His journey illustrates the possibilities available to emerging Indian filmmakers.
The 2026 festival also places considerable emphasis on new voices across its film selections. It will feature
52 women filmmakers and 62 debut filmmakers
from India and abroad. Among them,
10 women filmmakers and 12 debut filmmakers
will feature in competitive sections.
Seven films from different countries, India's The Sledge and Birds on Ice among them,
will also compete in the
Best Debut Feature Films Competition
. Such platforms provide opportunities for first-time directors to present their work alongside established filmmakers.
IFFI creates space for talent at different stages of development. While some participants are learning the craft, others are seeking recognition for their first films. The festival brings them together, allowing fresh ideas and emerging voices to find wider audiences.
Indian Panorama: Films in Many Indian Languages
India's cinematic landscape is as varied as the communities and cultures that shape it. Beyond mainstream cinema, countless stories emerge from the country's regional languages and filmmaking traditions. Some explore familiar human experiences, while others reveal lives rarely represented on screen. Bringing these different perspectives together has long been an important part of IFFI.
Indian Panorama
, introduced in 1978, plays a central role in this effort. This flagship IFFI section showcases outstanding contemporary Indian
feature
and
non-feature films
.
Source: Ministry of Information and Broadcasting
Over the years, Indian Panorama has brought several distinctive regional narratives into the spotlight. At IFFI 2023, Manipuri documentary
Andro Dreams
opened the non-feature section. Directed by Meena Longjam, it followed an all-girls football club in rural Manipur. The film explored women's determination amid financial difficulties and deeply rooted social barriers. In 2024, the Ladakhi short film
Ghar Jaisa Kuch
achieved another milestone. It became the first Ladakhi film to open Indian Panorama's non-feature section. Director Harsh Sangani's film explored displacement, belonging and the longing for home.
The diversity continued in 2025, with films representing both established and lesser-represented cinematic traditions. Tamil film
Amaran
was selected to open the feature section, and Hindi film
Kakori
the non-feature section. Selections also included
Vimukt
in Braj
,
Imbu
in Tulu
and
Oitharei
in Manipuri
. These films reflected the growing linguistic range of stories presented through Indian Panorama.
The
57th IFFI
carries this tradition forward with
25 feature and 20 non-feature films
. These were selected from
404
feature entries and
358
non-feature entries, respectively. In all, the Indian Cinema section will screen
76 films
in
18 languages
. The Ladakhi film
Becoming
, directed by Leena Yadav, will open the non-feature section alongside the opening feature film
Dhurandhar
, directed by Aditya Dhar. Other selections include
Urum
in Nyishi
,
Pili Channe
in Tulu
and
Birds on Ice
in Ladakhi
. The festival will also highlight
Marathi
and
Malayalam
cinema, celebrating their legacies and contemporary voices.
Pili Channe
Birds on Ice
Such selections demonstrate the importance of making room for different voices within Indian cinema. A regional film can introduce audiences to unfamiliar landscapes, traditions and experiences. Yet, its underlying themes may remain deeply relatable. By bringing these stories together, Indian Panorama broadens the understanding of India's cinematic identity. It also gives filmmakers a platform to connect with audiences beyond their immediate regions.
WAVES Film Bazaar and the BRICS Showcase
A film's journey does not end when the final scene is shot. Reaching audiences often requires financial support, industry connections and opportunities beyond familiar markets. For independent filmmakers, finding these opportunities can be particularly difficult. Over the years, IFFI has evolved into a space where such connections can take shape.
One such platform is
WAVES Film Bazaar
, which celebrates its
20th edition in 2026
. Established in 2007, it is
South Asia's largest film market
, held alongside IFFI in Goa. Unlike a traditional film festival, Film Bazaar focuses on the business and development of cinema. It brings together filmmakers, producers, financiers, distributors and other industry professionals from across the world. Its aim is to help promising film projects find the support needed to reach audiences.
A promising script may need a producer, while an unfinished film may need expert guidance. Another may be ready for distribution but lack access to international buyers. Film Bazaar addresses these different needs through specialised programmes. Its
Co-Production Market
connects projects with potential collaborators and financiers. The
Screenwriters' Lab
supports writers, while the
Work-in-Progress Lab
helps filmmakers refine their films. The
Viewing Room
, market screenings and a
Producers' Lab
help filmmakers connect with potential buyers and distributors.
The impact of these efforts can be traced through films associated with the platform.
The Lunchbox, Court, Newton
and
Girls Will Be Girls
are among the acclaimed films whose journeys it has contributed to. As Film Bazaar completes two decades, its significance extends beyond individual films. It represents a growing network of opportunities for Indian storytellers seeking international collaborations and audiences.
While Film Bazaar helps films reach new markets, cinema also connects nations through shared experiences. This cultural dimension finds expression in
IFFI's BRICS cinema showcase
, featuring
21 films in 2026
. Bringing together stories from BRICS nations, the programme explores different histories, societies and contemporary realities. It offers audiences opportunities to encounter perspectives shaped by experiences beyond their own.
The selection reflects both the diversity of these societies and the concerns connecting them. Brazil's
Amadeo and the Hypothetical New World
revisits the struggle against slavery. Indonesia's
The Sea Speaks His Name
follows the disappearance of a student activist during the country's 1998 people's movement. South Africa's
The Trek
examines the injustices of the colonial frontier. Though rooted in different histories, these films explore questions of freedom, identity and belonging.
Other films turn towards experiences closer to everyday life.
Dreaming of Serenada
, a Uganda-UK documentary, approaches climate change through a father-daughter relationship. China's
Embers
reflects on grief, loss and mortality. Such narratives demonstrate how personal experiences can illuminate larger social concerns. They also reveal how stories from different societies can find common emotional ground.
Dreaming of Serenada
Embers
The BRICS showcase reflects cinema's role in fostering
cultural understanding and dialogue among nations
. It creates space for stories that may otherwise remain unfamiliar to international audiences. Alongside Film Bazaar, it adds another dimension to IFFI's growing global engagement. While one builds professional connections, the other encourages conversations through films and storytelling.
Together, these platforms reflect how IFFI's influence extends beyond the festival's nine days. They bring new possibilities for filmmakers and fresh perspectives for audiences. More importantly, they demonstrate how cinema can connect people through both
collaboration and shared experiences
.
A Festival Where Stories Begin New Journeys
A film festival is more than its screenings, awards and celebrations. It also creates opportunities and connections that continue beyond the festival. For emerging filmmakers, these encounters can open doors to new possibilities. For regional and independent cinema, they offer a chance to reach wider audiences. Together, these opportunities contribute to an increasingly diverse and globally connected Indian film industry.
The theme
Stories Without Borders
reflects this, in the stories audiences experience and in the work of those who make them. As the
57th IFFI
brings together talent, creativity and cultures, it reinforces cinema's power to connect. A festival's lasting contribution lies in the films it showcases and in what those films and their creators go on to do.

title: India’s Electronics Exports Gain Momentum
subtitle: Non-Smartphone Products Emerge as a Strong Growth Engine
date:

content:
India’s electronic goods exports grew by
44% to US$ 31.97 billion
during April-September 2026-27. Smartphones remained the largest export segment, with shipments rising 35.8% to US$   18.17 billion.
Non-smartphone electronics
recorded faster
growth of 56.5%
, reaching $13.79 billion and increasing their share of total electronics exports to 43.2%. Key products included printed circuit boards, network transmission equipment, memory integrated circuits and storage devices. Strong export growth across these segments, with markets including Singapore, China, Hong Kong and Malaysia, reflects the broadening of India’s electronics export basket and growing presence in global markets.
Electronics Exports Register Strong Growth
India’s electronic goods exports continued to demonstrate strong momentum during
April-September 2026-27
, rising
44.0%
from
US$ 22.20 billion to US$ 31.97 billion
. While smartphones remained the largest component of the electronics export basket, the
period witnessed significantly faster growth in non-smartphone electronics
. This indicates a broadening of India’s electronics export base across components, circuit boards, communication equipment, memory products and storage devices.
Non-Smartphone Electronics Drive Export Diversification
A particularly strong story emerged from the
non-smartphone electronics segment
, where exports
increased by 56.5%, from US$ 8.81 billion to US$ 13.79 billion
. Consequently, the segment’s
share in India’s total electronic goods exports increased from 39.7% to 43.2%
, reflecting an increasingly diversified electronics export basket.
The expansion was supported by sharp gains across several key commodities.
Parts and Accessories- Mounted Printed Circuit Boards
Exports surged from
US$ 63.3 million to US$ 2.10 billion
, growing by
3219%
, with Singapore emerging as the dominant destination at US$ 1.87 billion, followed by China at US$ 111.5 million.
Populated, Loaded or Stuffed Printed Circuit Boards
Exports also expanded strongly,
increasing from US$ 213.7 million to US$ 864.1 million
, growing by
304%
. China was the
leading market at US$ 789.2 million
, while exports to Hong Kong increased from US$ 5.9 million to US$ 25.3 million.
Network Transmission and Routing Equipment
Exports
nearly doubled from US$ 732.9 million to US$ 1.45 billion
, growing by
98%
. The increase was led by
Hong Kong
, where exports
rose from US$ 264.7 million to US$ 857.7 million
. The United States and the Netherlands were also important markets at US$ 130.9 million and US$ 124.4 million, respectively.
Memory Integrated Circuits
Exports witnessed particularly rapid expansion, rising from just
US$ 23.1 million to US$ 562.4 million
, growing by
2333%
. Malaysia emerged as the largest destination at US$ 390.8 million, followed by Singapore at US$ 102.4 million and Hong Kong at US$ 25.2 million.
Solid-State Non-Volatile Storage Devices
Exports increased sharply from
US$ 14.6 million to US$ 260.5 million
, growing by
1680%
. China led the growth with exports reaching US$ 108.6 million. This was followed by Singapore at US$ 76.8 million, Hong Kong at US$ 22.3 million and the United States at US$ 20.7 million.
Smartphone Exports Rise
India’s exports of smartphones increased from
US$ 13.38 billion in April- September 2025-26 to US$ 18.17 billion in April- September 2026-27
, registering strong growth of 35.8%.
Smartphones continued to account for the
majority of India’s electronic goods exports
, although their share moderated from 60.3% to 56.8%. This moderation came amid even stronger growth in other segments of the electronics export basket.
Strengthening India’s Position in Global Electronics Trade
Taken together, the trends point to a
broader and increasingly diversified electronics export basket
. Smartphones continue to provide a strong foundation, with exports reaching US$ 18.17 billion, while
non-smartphone electronics are expanding at a faster pace
and
increasing their contribution to overall electronics exports.
The sharp growth across
printed circuit boards
,
communication equipment
,
memories
and
solid-state storage devices
, alongside expansion into markets such as Singapore, China, Hong Kong and Malaysia, highlights the growing contribution of non-smartphone products to India’s electronics export momentum.

title: IPFT, Gurugram, Achieves NABL Accreditation for Biostimulant Testing under ISO/IEC 17025:2017
subtitle: Strengthens national capacity for quality assurance and regulatory testing of Biostimulants
ministry: Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers :Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals
date:
प्रविष्टि तिथि:

content:
The Institute of Pesticide Formulation Technology (IPFT), Gurugram, an autonomous institute under the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Government of India, has achieved a significant milestone by securing accreditation from the National Accreditation Board for Testing and Calibration Laboratories (NABL) under ISO/IEC 17025:2017 for its biostimulant testing and analytical facilities.
The accreditation certificate, bearing Certificate No. NABLT1026HR19813 (in lieu of TC-14306), is valid up to 15 August 2030. This accreditation recognises the Institute's technical competence and quality management systems for the testing activities covered under its approved scope.
The achievement follows the Government of India's Gazette Notification No. 4242, dated 25 September 2025, issued under the Fertilizer (Inorganic, Organic or Mixed) (Control) Order, 1985. Under Clause 29(1C) of the Order, IPFT, Gurugram, was designated for the analysis of biostimulant samples collected by Inspectors in accordance with the prescribed procedure under Part C of Schedule VI.
Pursuant to this statutory recognition, IPFT undertook focused initiatives to strengthen its laboratory infrastructure, analytical methodologies, quality management systems and technical competence in accordance with ISO/IEC 17025:2017 and the applicable requirements of the Fertiliser (Inorganic, Organic or Mixed) (Control) Order, 1985.
The Institute systematically strengthened its analytical capabilities, testing protocols, quality assurance practices and laboratory management systems, culminating in the achievement of NABL accreditation.
This accomplishment reflects the collective commitment and dedicated efforts of the scientists, technical personnel, quality management team and supporting staff of IPFT. Their sustained efforts and scientific contributions have played a pivotal role in achieving this important institutional milestone.
The accreditation is expected to further strengthen the reliability and credibility of biostimulant testing and contribute to quality assurance, regulatory compliance and the effective implementation of the regulatory framework governing biostimulants in India. It also reinforces IPFT's commitment to providing scientifically robust analytical services to government agencies, regulatory authorities, industry and other stakeholders in the agricultural sector.
From statutory recognition through the Government Gazette to accreditation under an internationally recognized laboratory quality standard, this achievement represents an important step in IPFT's continuing efforts towards scientific excellence and institutional strengthening.
The Institute of Pesticide Formulation Technology (IPFT), Gurugram, is an autonomous institute under the Department of Chemicals and Petrochemicals, Ministry of Chemicals and Fertilizers, Government of India.
Established in 1991, the Institute is dedicated to research and development in pesticide formulation science and technology, analytical characterization, bio-evaluation and pilot-scale demonstration. IPFT provides scientific and technical support to the agrochemical sector through research, analytical testing, regulatory studies and technology development.
